ai-at-work.title: What’s behind the AI industry’s latest warnings of doom?
ai-at-work.excerpt: On Equity, we discussed the AI industry's latest debate about whether it poses an existential threat to humanity.
ai-at-work.dwp_take: The AI industry is having another round of public hand-wringing about existential risk while simultaneously trying to convince regulators not to actually regulate anything. This matters to digital workplace folks because these aren't just philosophical debates: AI vendors are pushing tools into your org while the people building them are apparently unsure if those tools will eventually turn on us all. Nothing says "buy our enterprise solution" quite like "by the way, this might threaten humanity's existence, but also we need minimal oversight."

ai-at-work.title: Obama urges Democrats to have a ‘clear plan’ for AI safeguards
ai-at-work.excerpt: Obama recently said that Democrats need to make artificial intelligence one of their “central agendas” and “have a very clear plan” to address concerns around the technology’s economic impact and safe
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Obama's calling on Democrats to develop a concrete AI policy framework focused on economic impact and safety concerns rather than just reacting to the tech. This matters because workplace leaders are already scrambling to implement AI tools without clear regulatory guidance, leaving them exposed to compliance risks and employee trust issues. Here's the thing though: politicians talking about having a plan and actually executing one are two different animals, so don't hold your breath waiting for clear guardrails before your CEO pushes another AI rollout.

ai-at-work.title: Sam Altman and Elon Musk back Dario Amodei’s call to slow down the frontier of AI development
ai-at-work.excerpt: Anthropic PBC Chief Executive Dario Amodei has once again called for the artificial intelligence industry to slow down the pace of frontier model development, only this time he’s being backed by two b
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Dario Amodei from Anthropic is calling for the AI industry to pump the brakes on frontier model development, and he's suddenly got powerful allies in Sam Altman and Elon Musk backing him up. This matters because workplace AI tools are rolling out faster than most organizations can actually implement them responsibly, and when the big players start saying "slow down," it signals real concerns about safety and sustainability. Of course, this is also the tech equivalent of three billionaires agreeing to go slower while they're all still racing full throttle, so I'll believe it when I see it reflected in actual product release schedules.

ai-at-work.title: Supio’s long-horizon agents point to a new operating model for law firms
ai-at-work.excerpt: The next phase of artificial intelligence in legal technology will not be defined by a better chatbot or a faster document-summarization tool. It will be defined by whether AI systems can take respons
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Supio is developing AI agents that can handle multi-day legal tasks across different systems and channels, then hand work back to attorneys for decision-making. This matters to digital workplace pros because it shows the next wave of AI isn't about replacing humans but creating new workflows that require thoughtful handoff points and integration strategies. If law firms are betting on this model, expect your boss to suddenly get very interested in how AI agents integrate with your actual tools and processes instead of just bolting on another chatbot that nobody uses.

digital-culture.title: Traveling to Europe? Beware of the credit card trap that’s costing tourists big money
digital-culture.excerpt: I just returned from a family vacation through France, Spain, and Portugal, and we had an amazing time. However, I couldn’t help but notice a new tourist trap that could have potentially cost me hundr
digital-culture.dwp_take: Dynamic Currency Conversion is when merchants abroad offer to charge your credit card in your home currency instead of the local one, typically at terrible exchange rates that pad their profits. This matters to digital workplace professionals because remote work and business travel are now standard, and getting ripped off on currency conversions adds real costs to expense reports and personal finances. My advice: always decline DCC and let your card's issuer handle the exchange, unless you enjoy giving your money away to some tourist trap merchant with a smile.

digital-culture.title: AI Has Human Doctors Asking: What’s Left for Us?
digital-culture.excerpt: A recent paper argues that AI is often better at doctoring than doctors. Guess who isn't thrilled.
digital-culture.dwp_take: A new research paper claims AI outperforms human doctors at certain diagnostic tasks, sparking real anxiety in the medical profession about their future relevance. This matters to digital workplace professionals because it's the exact same disruption curve hitting knowledge workers everywhere, and your organization is probably having the same conversations about AI replacing your experts right now. Here's the thing though: doctors are asking the right question, which means they might actually survive this better than the ones pretending AI is just a fancy calculator.

industry-news.title: Nothing OS 5 Ends Support for Three Phones: What Owners Should Do Next
industry-news.excerpt: Nothing OS 5 leaves three phones without Android 17. See which Nothing devices are affected, what support remains, and whether owners should upgrade. The post Nothing OS 5 Ends Support for Three Phone
industry-news.dwp_take: Nothing dropped support for three of its older phones with OS 5, leaving those devices stuck on older Android versions. This matters because digital workplace pros managing BYOD programs need to know which devices will fall out of security patch cycles and become compliance risks on their networks. Honestly, this is why I tell companies to stop pretending they can support every phone ever made and instead maintain a published list of approved devices with known EOL dates.

industry-news.title: Microsoft May Soon Fix Windows 11’s Obvious Dark Mode Automation Gap
industry-news.excerpt: Microsoft is testing automatic Light and Dark Mode switching in Windows 11, with scheduling based on sunrise, sunset, fixed times, or PC activity. The post Microsoft May Soon Fix Windows 11’s Obvious
industry-news.dwp_take: Microsoft is finally adding automatic light and dark mode switching to Windows 11 based on time of day, sunrise/sunset, or device activity. This matters because workplace IT teams spend ridiculous amounts of time fielding complaints about eye strain and accessibility issues that a simple automation should have solved years ago. Honestly, it's wild that this basic feature took this long to arrive, but I guess at least someone at Redmond finally realized that not everyone works in a cave.

industry-news.title: How small-business leaders can work anywhere more securely with Dell Pro laptops
industry-news.excerpt: A modern secure, workplace needs modern, secure laptops. We take a look at the security features available with the Dell Pro range of business laptops.
industry-news.dwp_take: Dell published a marketing piece highlighting security features in their Pro laptop lineup aimed at small-business leaders. This matters because remote work security is genuinely where most breaches happen, and having solid hardware with built-in protections is table stakes for any organization not wanting to become a cautionary tale. Look, I've seen too many small businesses get compromised because someone was running a five-year-old laptop with security updates they never installed, so Dell's angle here is fair even if the article itself reads like it was focus-grouped by a committee.

industry-news.title: Atlassian introduces 'always-on' capabilities for agentic development workflows
industry-news.excerpt: Customers can now adopt and scale governed agentic workflows right across the AI software development lifecycle
industry-news.dwp_take: Atlassian added autonomous agent capabilities to their development platform so teams can automate workflows across the entire software creation process with built-in governance controls. This matters because most organizations are still figuring out how to safely deploy AI agents in real work without creating chaos or compliance nightmares, and having guardrails baked in from the start beats bolting them on later. That said, I'll believe "always-on" actually works smoothly in production when I see it. The gap between what vendors demo and what teams actually manage in the wild is usually measured in miles.
